Build G1 and G2 by integer arithmetic, tile the cell m/p times along the seam, then solve the two corner caps (where the seam meets the walls at bottom-left and top-right) as small window problems with the windowfill engine and walls added. Count N. Keep (n, L) when N >= n and L < our side. Keep surplus squares as slack for sqpack and fq polish. Interface: seamcell cells --f-range 0.5:0.95 --pmax 8 > cells.jsonl. seamcell build --cells cells.jsonl --n 300:1000 --cur results/assembled-*-per-n.tsv --out cand/. Each candidate is written as Evan's 'n s / x y deg' text plus a Kaggle CSV, then goes through ulpcert, floatsafe.py, and pdscore.py or score.py before it counts.
tools.expected_gain: 0.00 to 0.07. Expected value about 0.02 (25 to 35% chance it works at all).
tools.gain_reasoning: About 0.16 of the 0.170 gap sits at n >= 200, where the bests are two-grid-plus-seam layouts. The leader families fit waste of about 0.94 to 0.98 per step against our 1.04, and that waste difference alone reproduces our gap at n=498 to three digits. If seamcell finds cells as good as the leader's, the families (the top 30 fractional parts carry about 34% of the gap, about 0.057) come out in one sweep. Its cells also seed compose2 and FTMC for the 146 single-member families. Why it may fail: the real channels may not be periodic, because the caps and multi-angle relaxations may carry the gain. That is the same reason bandseed.py's rigid single-angle fill stopped at 492 of 498. I give it under 35% because nobody has published a cell. Cats batch-releasing a whole family on 11-01 is the main evidence that a construction like this exists.
tools.first_test: Day 1, on one boxB core, cell solver only. (a) Positive control: fold our own n=498 seam (54 tilted squares at about 25.3 degrees) modulo T_p for p = 1..6. The solver must return a cell whose waste per step is at or below our 1.040 at f <= 0.8231. If it cannot rebuild what we already hold, stop. (b) Discovery test: run the enumeration over f in [0.55, 0.85]. Success means a rigid cell with waste per step <= 0.985, or a jammed f* within 1e-5 of 0.79386 or 0.60588, the leader's fractional parts. A hit is strong evidence that we found the leader's island, and it costs hours. (c) Only then build n=498 and n=544 end to end and compare with 22.7939 and 23.7941.
tools.risks: The seam may be quasi-periodic, or the gain may sit in the caps, so the cell optimum transfers poorly. The separator-assignment MILP grows as 8^pairs, so p > 6 may need pruning by contact distance. NLP solutions with near-zero clearance need dilation before certification, which costs about 1e-10 per n and is harmless. It overlaps FTMC and compose2 as a seed source, which is a plus as long as the lane wires the cells into compose2 pieces instead of keeping a separate pipeline.

tools.name: windowfill: fixed-side window MINLP insertion with contact-graph flips
tools.purpose: Answer the real question behind 'one or two squares short': at the target side L* from the per-puzzle board, can a local window of our n-1 packing hold one more square? The engine re-solves the window's tilted squares, discrete separator choices included, which neither sqpack (side shrink only) nor FTMC (re-solves the upright count exactly, while the tilted squares only get Monte Carlo moves) does. It is also the cap solver for seamcell.
tools.design: Language: Rust (window extraction, slack map, NLP inner loop through an augmented-Lagrangian L-BFGS-B with analytic gradients) plus HiGHS MILP from Python. Steps. (1) Scale our n-1 packing to side L*, which fits by definition. Compute a slack map: free-space polygons from box minus union of squares (exact polygon clipping with the i_overlay crate), aggregated with a Gaussian kernel of radius 2.5. Free area at the best side is 21 to 30 units for n = 498 to 971, so about 0.9 to 1.3 units of it sit within radius 3 of most seam points. Take the top 20 windows by local free area, mostly seam windows. (2) Window W = the squares whose centre is within r of the window centre (r = 2.5 to 3.5, so k_W = 8 to 25). Everything outside W is a fixed obstacle. Add 1 new square. (3) Phase A, a MILP over the disjunctions: binary separator per near pair (axis-aligned obstacles make most pairs 4-way), positions linearised around a few discrete angle candidates for the new square (0 degrees, the band angle, the angles of its neighbours, 45 degrees), with an L-infinity trust region on each mover and the objective max t, the common clearance. (4) Phase B, an NLP with those separators fixed: maximise t with exact projections. t >= 0 means feasible. (5) When the NLP fails, add a no-good cut on the separator pattern, plus a 'nearest topology' neighbourhood: flip the separators the kkt tool flags as degenerate first. Budget per window: 60 s. (6) On success, the n squares at L* go to sqpack and fq polish, then ulpcert, floatsafe.py and the official metric. Interface: windowfill --pack ours_n-1.txt --side L* --add 1 --windows 20 --r 3 --budget 60 --out found/. It also exposes a library function solve_window(fixed_obstacles, movers, walls, k_new, periodic=None), which seamcell calls for caps. Scheduler: rank n by (gap x P(success)), where P grows with local free area in the top window. Run 1-short puzzles first (305 puzzles, 0.0995 of the gap).
tools.gain_reasoning: Insertion at L* is exactly the 1-short problem (0.0995 over 305 puzzles). But a window of radius 3 can only reach the slack inside it. The local free area is around 1 unit, which is marginal, and many 1-short puzzles probably need the slack moved along the whole seam, which is what seamcell or FTMC does. Tiago Cabo's SLP and the research's hole-growing LP (ranked 2-6%, weak) both fail for lack of discrete flips. The separator MILP is the part they lacked, so I put this above them but well below seamcell. I expect wins mainly where our seam has a local defect, a few dozen puzzles at about 1e-4 each.
tools.first_test: Positive control, the test the band-end grinder failed (1,159 tries, 0 restorations, per the README). Take our n=803, remove one tilted band-end square, keep side 28.xxx unchanged, and run windowfill on that window with a 15-minute budget. It must put a square back at clearance >= 0, certified by the metric. Second control: remove an upright from deep inside a grid. It must restore that one trivially. Negative control: run at L* - 0.05 on n=498, where the area cannot fit. It must report infeasible and never output a packing that score.py rejects. Then the real run: the 20 one-short puzzles with the largest top-window free area, 10 CPU-minutes each, on one box.
tools.risks: The slack may be too spread out for any radius-3 window. The real-run test measures exactly that and kills the tool cheaply if so. MILP size grows with k_W squared. Big-M linearisation of rotations is loose, so phase B is what matters. Under float64 the NLP returns contacts at about 1e-12, and every output must be dilated and certified by ulpcert and the official metric, never by the solver's own feasibility flag.

tools.name: kkt: active-set KKT certifier, flip oracle and polish gatekeeper
tools.purpose: Decide per n whether continuous moves can still help, and if not, which combinatorial move to try. For each packing it returns one of three verdicts. DESCENT: a first-order shrink exists, so polish. JAMMED-DEGENERATE: no descent, but some contacts have zero multipliers or ambiguous separators, and these are the flip candidates for windowfill. STRICT-LOCAL-MIN: first- and second-order conditions hold for every nearby separator assignment, so polishing is provably futile and the n leaves the polish queue. It also runs an exact Newton-KKT solve on the 19 puzzles within 1e-3.
tools.design: Python + scipy/HiGHS. Reuse rigid.py's linearisation (MIT, Donev-Torquato-Stillinger-Connelly style); do not rewrite it. Variables: z = (x_i, y_i, theta_i), s. The active set A covers walls (corner coordinate within delta of 0 or s, with the kink at axis-aligned angles split into one constraint per sign, as rigid.py does) and pairs (best separating edge line, gap < delta, with corner-corner near-contacts kept as disjunctions). delta goes 1e-9, 1e-7, 1e-5 to show the verdict is stable. Step 1, LP: min ds subject to J_A dz + g_A >= 0, |dz|_inf <= R. If ds* < -1e-12 the verdict is DESCENT, and the tool hands dz to sqpack or fq. Step 2, duals: lambda from the LP at ds* = 0 (HiGHS gives row duals). Contacts with lambda <= tol are degenerate. Step 3, second order: Z = null space of the strongly active rows (lambda > tol). If the minimum eigenvalue of Z^T (sum lambda_c grad^2 g_c) Z is > 0 with a margin, the point is a strict local minimum for that contact graph. The constraint Hessians are analytic: corner projections are trigonometric in theta. Step 4, disjunction scan: for each of up to d <= 12 ambiguous pairs (corner-corner, or two separators within delta), rerun step 1 under each alternative separator (rigid.py's axis-choice restriction is exactly what can hide a descent). Do it exhaustively when 2^d <= 4096 and with a MILP otherwise, as in Evan's vv_branch_test. Verdict rule, which is how we decide flips versus continuous moves: continuous moves are exhausted only when every separator assignment gives ds* = 0 and the reduced Hessian is positive definite. If any assignment gives ds* < 0, take that flip and polish. If the problem is only degenerate (zero multipliers, singular reduced Hessian), there are flat directions along which a contact can be released at no cost. Hand those contacts to windowfill as the windows to try first. Step 5, Newton-KKT: for the 19 puzzles within 1e-3, solve the square KKT system on the fixed active set with mpmath at 50 digits, then dilate. This is the exact last-digit polish (research idea 10), done once. Interface: kkt classify --pack n.txt --> {verdict, ds*, n_active, n_degenerate, flip_candidates:[(i,j,alt_sep)], min_eig}. kkt sweep --best DIR --> kkt.tsv, which the drivers' n-picker reads to skip STRICT-LOCAL-MIN puzzles.
tools.expected_gain: Direct about 0.0001 to 0.0005 (hard ceiling 0.00049). Indirect: frees most of the polish CPU and ranks flip windows.
tools.gain_reasoning: The ceiling is measured: only 19 puzzles trail by less than 1e-3 in side, worth 0.00049 in total, and none within 1e-6. Continuous moves on a fixed graph cannot cover a 0.009 median side gap on a jammed packing. The value is that a STRICT-LOCAL-MIN verdict turns 'polish found nothing in 180 s' (a guess) into a proof. The drivers spent about 24 threads x 31 h for 0.0011. If kkt marks most of the 416 trailing puzzles as strict minima, those threads move to seamcell, windowfill and FTMC with evidence behind the move.
tools.first_test: Controls before any sweep. (1) Positive: take n=10 at its known optimum 3.70710678118654, scale it by 1 + 1e-4 and jitter it by 1e-5. kkt must report DESCENT and Newton-KKT must return to within 1e-12 of 3.70710678118654. (2) Negative: the exact n=10 optimum must come out STRICT-LOCAL-MIN or JAMMED-DEGENERATE, never DESCENT. (3) Mutation: flip one separator by hand in a jammed packing and check that step 4 detects the alternative. Then sweep our 1,000 packings in 1-2 CPU-hours on boxB and report the verdict counts plus the step-5 result on the 19 near puzzles.
tools.risks: Degeneracy is the norm in jammed square packings: rattlers, and grid rows with zero multipliers. Many puzzles may land in JAMMED-DEGENERATE rather than a clean verdict, and the rattler filter (squares free to move without changing ds) has to come first. Duals from an interior-point LP need crossover to be exact; use simplex. The verdict is local and says nothing about other basins, so it may only remove n from the polish queue, never from the combinatorial queues.

tools.name: ulpcert: fast, sound float64-robust certifier for search inner loops and submissions
tools.purpose: Replace the empirical check in floatsafe.py ('passes the metric after one pandas parse') with a proof: the packing is feasible for every float64 within +/-K ulps of each written value, and the side measured from the decimal strings equals the claimed one. It also has to be fast enough (well under 1 ms per 1,000-square packing) to run inside seamcell and windowfill, so candidates are certified at generation time instead of waiting minutes for the mpmath metric.
tools.design: Rust, single binary plus a Python wrapper. Rigorous error bounds on top of float64, with no FPU rounding-mode switching (that is not portable on Apple silicon, and inari is x86-only). (1) Inputs: the written decimal strings. Parse each with Rust's correctly rounded parser into v, then form [v - K ulp(v), v + K ulp(v)] with K = 8 (covers pandas' default 'high' parser, which can be 1 ulp off, plus any to_csv round trip). (2) sin/cos: reduce the angle against a double-double 2*pi. Evaluate in double-double, or use libm with a bound of 2 ulp checked by the test suite against mpmath over 1e7 random angles. Widen by the angle interval width (|d sin| <= |d theta|). (3) Pair test on the metric's 4 SAT axes. Each projection is a sum of at most 6 products of magnitude <= 50, so the a priori float error is below gamma_6 x 50 x 4 ≈ 1e-13. Certify 'separated' when the computed gap minus the interval widths minus 1e-13 is > 0. Pairs with a margin below 1e-12 go to mpmath at 50 digits, the same interval code as kaggle_metric.py. (4) Side: max-min of the corner coordinates in double-double, compared with the metric's L_DPS measurement on a random 1% of puzzles. (5) Clearance report: the minimum certified gap per n and the worst pair. (6) Repair, only when certification fails: centre dilation 1 + e about the centroid, the smallest e from 1e-15 upward, as floatsafe.py does today. The side cost at 2e-11 clearance is about L x 4e-11/sqrt(n) per n, about 1e-8 in total, so a cleverer per-pair LP repair is not worth building. Interface: ulpcert check sub.csv --K 8 --> per-n {ok, min_gap, worst_pair, L}. ulpcert fix in.csv out.csv --min-gap 2e-11. ulpcert check-one --pack n.txt (library call for the search tools). floatsafe.py keeps its role as the last step; ulpcert runs before it and is the hard gate.
tools.expected_gain: 0.000 score. It is insurance against a repeat of the 25.974 submission (a 3.75-point loss), and it speeds up candidate verification.
tools.gain_reasoning: The current floatsafe.py file scored 22.2223 on Kaggle, so today's path works empirically, and the clearance it adds costs only about 1e-8. ulpcert adds no packings. It turns 'it passed once on Kaggle' into a proof that holds whatever the Kaggle loader does with the last ulp. Its speed is what lets seamcell and windowfill check thousands of candidates per second. It also settles whether Samanyu's 'Kaggle rejects 1e-12 gaps' report concerns parsing at all: an ulp at coordinate 30 is 3.6e-15, so a 1e-12 gap should be robust to +/-8 ulps, and if it is not, the cause is elsewhere.
tools.first_test: (1) Agreement: run it on gather/floatsafe-2026-11-08.csv, which Kaggle scored 22.2223365. All 1,000 n must come back ok and L must match the official metric to 1e-40. (2) Negative controls: the first submission assembled-2026-11-08.csv, which scored 25.974 on Kaggle. ulpcert must flag the 190 exact-contact puzzles before any repair. Also move one square of n=2 by 1e-14 into its neighbour: it must fail. (3) Mutation: weaken the error bound to 0 in a debug build and confirm that at least one control then wrongly passes, which proves the bound is load-bearing. (4) Speed: n=1000 checked in under 1 ms on a boxB core.
tools.risks: The sin/cos error bound rests on libm behaviour checked by testing, not proved. The double-double path removes that dependence and should be the default. Any disagreement with the official metric is resolved in favour of the metric, and ulpcert then gets fixed; it never overrides pdscore.py or score.py.

critique.angle: Adversarial critique of the exact and continuous optimisation angle (seamcell, windowfill, kkt, ulpcert). I checked it against the lane files and against Evan's repo on boxA (read-only: ext/evand/search). I recomputed from results/assembled-2026-11-08-per-n.tsv and per-puzzle-lb-2026-11-07.json. The trailing-puzzle facts hold: total gap 0.1704. 29 puzzles trail by less than 1e-9, all float ties worth 4e-11 together. 19 trail by between 1e-9 and 1e-3, worth 0.00049. The median shortfall is 0.0084 and the 90th percentile 0.0197. So the ceiling on continuous polish is real. Two of the angle's arguments do not hold. (1) 'Waste per step' is defined as (L^2 - n)/m, so it is the side written another way. The claim that '0.06 x m/(2L) reproduces our gap at n=498' is an identity, not evidence that seams explain the gap. (2) The evidence that does support a periodic seam is one the angle fitted wrong. In the m+0.794 family (n = 299, 454, 498, 544, 747, 803) the leader's count fits n - m^2 = 0.82m - 3.9 with residuals under 0.3. The angle's fit was 0.65m. That means about 0.82 extra squares per diagonal step, plus a fixed cap cost of about 3.9 squares. A structure whose count grows linearly in m is a periodic seam, not a fixed island. That is the only real support in this angle for building anything new. Duplication checks in Evan's repo: exact/localmin.py already issues local-minimum certificates (strictly positive contact forces), on top of rigid.py, nlpdesc.py, exactsolve.vv_branch_test, inc.py, satcheck_f64.py and dilate_cert.py. harden.py already has an 'insert:K' transform: add K squares, reharden, then fq polish. layout.py builds channel layouts with the exact axis fill. quadrant_lp, seam_1d and SEAM_W1.md cover periodic seam capacity, but only as LP bounds. None of them builds a cell. The two named families carry only 0.0095 of the gap (0.0055 and 0.0040). The band regime as a whole (n >= 200, fractional side in 0.5 to 0.9) carries 0.142. So seamcell pays off only if it yields a gain-versus-f curve that transfers across that whole regime. Fitting the two families alone is not enough.

verdicts.name: seamcell: periodic seam-cell optimiser and full-n constructor
verdicts.corrected_gain: 0.00 to 0.05; expected value about 0.01. P(working cell) about 25%. The two named families alone are worth 0.0095. The rest needs the cell to carry over to other f across the 0.142 band-regime gap, and the 19 teams between us and Cats probably hold part of that already.
verdicts.reasons: It is the only tool in this angle aimed at the place the gap lives: adding squares at a fixed side through a structure that scales with m. Nothing in the lane or in Evan's repo solves a periodic seam cell. layout.py builds non-periodic channel rows, and quadrant_lp/seam_1d are dual bounds, not constructions. The leader's 0.794 family fits n - m^2 = 0.82m - 3.9 tightly over 6 members, which supports the periodic premise better than the angle's own waste-per-step argument (that one is circular). Weak points: the 3.5-day Rust plus Benders build is unrealistic. An 8^pairs separator MILP for k up to 19 squares will not finish. The caps are where the -3.9 constant lives, and they are handed to windowfill, which I reject. The gain case is also inflated by counting all 0.057 of the top-30 fractional parts as reachable.
verdicts.improvements: Make the discovery target sharp and falsifiable. At f = 0.79386, find a periodic seam cell whose net gain is about 0.82 squares per diagonal step. Fit the same law (slope and cap constant) on the 0.6059 family, (n - m^2)/m of about 0.25, and use it as a second target. Prototype in Python on Evan's fixed-line NLP (nlpdesc.py through ipenv.sh/cyipopt), with periodic images added. Re-pick the separator lines at each NLP point, as nlpdesc does, plus multistart, and drop the full MILP enumeration. Port to Rust only once a cell beats our seam. Cap p at 6. Run the positive control first: fold our own n=498 seam and get our 1.04 back. Do caps and assembly with Evan's compose2/mis_fill2 exact upright fill plus fq polish, not a new window engine. Day 1 is the cell solver only, with a kill rule: if no cell reaches 0.75 gain per step at f = 0.794 within a day of one-box compute, stop. Validate end to end on 299 (smallest member, 17.7936) before 498/544, then carry the result up the family. Every output goes through floatsafe.py and pdscore.py, which already enforce the 2e-11 clearance. Build estimate: about 2 days to a go/no-go answer on the cell, then 2 to 3 days to build all n.

verdicts.name: windowfill: fixed-side window MINLP insertion with contact-graph flips
verdicts.reasons: The angle's own numbers sink it: about 1 unit of free area within radius 3, spread as slivers 0.01 to 0.03 wide across a jammed packing. A 60 s MILP-plus-NLP over 8 to 25 movers with big-M rotations cannot gather a whole unit square from that. Freeing that room is a global rearrangement, which FTMC with its exact refill (already cloned, top-ranked in the research) is built for. Evan's harden.py 'insert:K' already does fixed-side insertion followed by rehardening and fq. The research ranks hole-growing insertion 2 to 6% and calls it mostly a duplicate of FTMC. The proposed positive control (re-insert a removed band-end square) is the one the outside grinder failed, but passing it says little about the real case, where the missing square never had a hole. The cap-solver role belongs in seamcell, through compose2/mis_fill2.
verdicts.improvements: Do not build it. If seamcell needs caps, use compose2/mis_fill2 plus fq. If someone still wants an insertion check, run harden.py --xform insert:1 at L* on 5 of our 1-short puzzles for an hour as a negative-or-positive probe before writing any code.

verdicts.name: kkt: active-set KKT certifier, flip oracle and polish gatekeeper
verdicts.corrected_gain: 0.0000 to 0.0005 direct (the measured ceiling); the CPU-freeing benefit is moot
verdicts.reasons: Most of it already exists in Evan's repo. rigid.py does the shrink LP and rigidity, exact/localmin.py issues grade-A local-minimum certificates from strictly positive contact forces, nlpdesc.py plus exactsolve.vv_branch_test do the MILP separator switches, and inc.py builds the incidence model. The CPU it would free is not worth proving futile. The polish drivers are about to stop under the 11-14 rule, and the research recommends stopping them now, so nobody needs a certificate to justify reallocating 24 threads. A local verdict also says nothing about the drivers' drop and grow modes. The exact Newton-KKT step on the 19 near puzzles is worth at most 0.00049, which matters only for tie-breaking at the end. Two days for that is poor value.
verdicts.improvements: If anything, a half-day wrapper that runs rigid.py and exact/localmin.py over our 1,000 packings and writes a TSV, used only to tie-break near the 2027-01-17 milestone. No new certifier.

verdicts.name: ulpcert: fast, sound float64-robust certifier for search inner loops and submissions
verdicts.reasons: The risk it insures against is already handled and shown on Kaggle. floatsafe.py enforces MIN_CLEARANCE = 2e-11 (floatsafe.py line 32) and checks after a pandas parse. That file scored 22.2223365 on Kaggle, matching pdscore locally. The ±8 ulp model is wrong: pandas parses a given string to one deterministic float64, and pdscore reproduces that read exactly, so there is nothing random to bound. The search tools do not need a sub-ms metric-grade check in their inner loop. They use their own overlap penalties, and Evan's satcheck_f64.py and dilate_cert.py (rational certificates) already cover a fast float check and a sound one. The design also contradicts itself: double-double cannot 'match the official metric to 1e-40'.
verdicts.improvements: Skip the build. At most, add a one-line per-n min-gap report to floatsafe.py's output (an hour), and keep pdscore.py as the gate before every submission.

design.angle: Search infrastructure and scheduling. The plain version: none of these tools adds a square on its own. They decide where FTMC, compose2 and transplant jobs run, keep every packing in one place across the boxes, and make sure every gain reaches Kaggle intact. What I checked: (1) The gap is flat. The largest single puzzle gap is 0.00135 (n=971). The top 113 puzzles hold 50.3% of the 0.1704 per-puzzle gap and the top 300 hold 91.4%, over 416 puzzles. Cats and boxes holds 0.146 of it. So any search has to win on 150 or more puzzles to matter, and spreading CPU by gap alone (what drive.py does) is close to uniform. The real lever is that the chance of success varies hugely by puzzle and method. (2) Evan's MIT repo on boxA already has most of the single-box machinery: pk/store.py (a sqlite store with dedup up to symmetry and provenance), pk/bandit.py (Thompson sampling per CPU-second), pk/credit.py (credit passed up the lineage), pk/tasks.py (a task pool) and pk/cpubudget.py. But cpubudget reads /proc, so it is Linux-only and fails on the macOS boxes. The store and pool are per box, and the bandit picks between move kinds inside one campaign, not across puzzles against a Kaggle target. So the missing piece is a fleet layer on top of his code, not a rewrite of it. (3) A gap I found in today's setup: drive.py splits n by n%3 across boxes, but its 'drop' and 'grow' starts read n+1 and n-1 from the box's own state dir. Those n belong to the other boxes, so 50% of jobs (drop 0.35 + grow 0.15) start from stale seed or harvest copies and never from the other boxes' improvements. A shared store fixes that. (4) The polish drivers are already stopped (the boxA STOP file is dated 11-09 01:41 and the log says it exited), so the fleet is free for whatever the lane runs next. I touched nothing on any box. (5) Fleet budget to the 2027-01-17 milestone is about 35 usable threads x 24 h x 69 days, roughly 58k CPU-hours. The old polish measured about 1.5e-6 score per CPU-hour (0.0011 over 31 h on about 24 threads). If FTMC needs 2-20 CPU-hours per puzzle, a full pass over 416 puzzles is 1k-8k CPU-hours. So by January, CPU is probably not the binding limit; method quality is. The scheduler's value is front-loaded: it finds within the first two weeks which method works in which regime, stops spending on dead cells, and pushes a family win to its siblings at once. My overall estimate: the four tools together add about 0.005-0.02 on top of what the engines find (which the research puts at 0.04-0.11), not 0.168. They also prevent a repeat of the 25.97 public score. Recommendation: build sqstore and sqgate first (2.5 days, safe value), and build sqfleet only once the lane's FTMC positive control passes. If FTMC fails that control, a scheduler has nothing worth scheduling. Summary: these tools make every CPU-hour count and every gain land safely, but they close the gap only as far as the search engines can; expect +0.005 to +0.02, plus insurance.

tools.name: sqstore: central packing store with Kaggle-grade certification
tools.purpose: One source of truth for every packing we hold or find, on all boxes and from all sources (our drivers, harvest, Evan's pk store, FTMC and compose2 output). Each packing carries a Kaggle-safety status, so the assembler reads only certified rows, and fresh n-1, n+1 and same-family packings reach every box as seeds. This fixes the stale drop/grow seeds that come from the n%3 split.
tools.design: Python 3.12, stdlib plus numpy; sqlite in WAL mode on boxA <data>. Tables: packing(id TEXT PRIMARY KEY = sha256 of the canonical form, n, side REAL, side_dec TEXT (50-digit side from the metric), score REAL, coords BLOB (float64 x,y,deg, canonical order), T (tilted count), frac = side - floor(side), status in {raw, metric_ok, pandas_ok, clear2e11_ok, rejected}, min_clearance REAL, created_utc); sighting(packing_id, source, method, box, run_id, cpu_s, licence, parent_id, utc), which keeps several sightings per packing as provenance; best(n, packing_id), a view over clear2e11_ok rows. Canonical form: translate to the box corner, apply all 8 D4 symmetries of the bounding box, normalise angles to [0,90), sort squares lexicographically on values rounded to 1e-9, hash the smallest of the 8 serialisations. This is the same dedup Evan's store does, written fresh so it does not depend on his schema. Certification pipeline (a function shared with sqgate): kaggle_metric.evaluate_single_puzzle on the text, then floatsafe's pandas path, then an exact SAT-gap check in Decimal for min clearance; if clearance < 2e-11, a centre dilation search reusing floatsafe's 1+e ladder, stored as a child packing with move='dilate'. Interfaces: CLI `sqstore ingest <path|state-dir|pk-store> --source S --method M` (CSV, per-n txt, JSON, Evan 'n s / x y deg'), `sqstore get n [--best|--parents|--family frac]`, `sqstore export-pk n` (writes into Evan's pk import format for compose2 pieces), `sqstore stats`. A small HTTP JSON endpoint (stdlib http.server on the private network, read-only GETs plus a POST /sink that queues ingest) so workers on the boxF and boxes push results without a shared filesystem. The writer is single (one ingest worker process), so sqlite concurrency is a non-issue.
tools.expected_gain: 0.001-0.004 directly; enabler for the rest
tools.gain_reasoning: Direct gains come from two things. (a) drop/grow starts then use the freshest n+/-1 from every box instead of stale seed copies. That is 50% of drive.py-style jobs today, but drop/grow polishing yields about 1e-6/CPU-h, so it is worth little unless FTMC uses n-1 parents. (b) A family hit at one n (e.g. 791, which shares fractional part .6370295589 with 908) is visible to every box the moment it lands. That is worth something only once sqfleet or a transplant job reads it. Most of the value is indirect: sqgate and sqfleet need it, and it removes the class of errors where a box overwrites a better import (already patched once in drive.py).
tools.first_test: Reproduce the 11-09 submission. Ingest the three state-*/best dirs, the harvest winners and gather/floatsafe-2026-11-08.csv. Then `sqstore stats` must report 1,000 certified n, and the assembled best must score 22.2223365223 through pdscore.py. That is 1e-10 tolerance against Kaggle's public number. Negative controls that must go red: (1) an n=2 with an overlap gets status rejected; (2) a copy of a public exact-contact packing (one of the 190) without floatsafe must fail pandas_ok; (3) a packing dilated only to 1e-12 must fail clear2e11_ok; (4) the same packing rotated 90 degrees and with its squares shuffled must dedup to the same id. If (4) yields two ids, canonicalisation is broken.
tools.risks: The canonical form may split near-duplicates that differ by 1e-10 polish into separate rows. That is harmless (they are separate parents) but inflates the count. It can be capped per n by keeping the best K per (n, frac). It would duplicate Evan's store, so keep the export-pk bridge one-way and never write into his store from ours. The licence column must carry the kmmmvs bundle's mixed terms through to the prize-claim export. Single host: if boxA is down, workers buffer results locally in a spool dir and resend.

tools.name: sqgate: auto re-assembly, float-safe certification, scoring and leaderboard diff
tools.purpose: Every certified improvement becomes a submission-ready file with a proven Kaggle score within minutes, and no file can leave our hands that has not passed the Kaggle-path checks. The public score of 25.974 on 11-08 is the failure this exists to make impossible. It also refreshes the per-puzzle target board, so the scheduler aims at today's targets, not the 11-07 board.
tools.design: Python, a single script driven by cron (launchd on boxA, every 15 min). Steps: (1) read sqstore best; if the total moved by >= 0.001 since the last candidate, or on demand, write candidate-<utc>.csv in id/n/square_id/x/y/angle form with exact float64 reprs; (2) run the full Kaggle twin: pandas default read_csv -> DataFrame -> the unchanged kaggle_metric.score, plus the 2e-11 min-clearance check per n, plus a row-count and id-contiguity check; (3) refuse the candidate (exit 1, written to a RED file) if any n is not ok, if the total is above the last submitted total, or if any n is worse than in the last submitted file; per-n regressions are listed; (4) write candidate.json (sha256, total, per-n diff vs last submitted, which n moved, by which method and source, licence summary); (5) read-only Kaggle CLI leaderboard plus a refresh of the per-puzzle board (inversion's per-puzzle board through the existing harvest_fetch path), stored as targets-<date>.json with team and date per n, and diffed against yesterday's: which n the field moved, by how much, and which teams. Submitting stays a manual step with a printed one-line command; the tool never calls `kaggle competitions submit`. Output: a short markdown report per run in logs/gate/.
tools.expected_gain: 0 in packings; insurance worth the 3.75 points already lost once, plus avoiding stale targets
tools.gain_reasoning: It closes none of the 0.168. Its value is that no future submission repeats the 22.22 -> 25.97 loss, and that Samanyu's 1e-12 clearance rejection (22.26 local -> 22.36 on Kaggle) is caught before upload rather than after. The refreshed board changes the scheduler's targets: teams submitted on 11-05 to 11-08, so some feasibility jobs today aim at a side that is no longer the frontier. Tie-breaking by earliest submission makes the latency gain near zero in score but nonzero near the end.
tools.first_test: Replay history. Feed it gather/assembled-2026-11-08.csv (the file that scored 25.974): it must go RED, with the about 190 exact-contact n listed. Feed it gather/floatsafe-2026-11-08.csv: GREEN, total 22.2223365223, matching the public score. Mutate one coordinate of n=498 by +1e-12 towards a neighbour: RED on clearance only. Make n=10 worse by 0.01 in a copy: RED with a per-n regression line. Each red must be watched failing before the gate is trusted.
tools.risks: The Kaggle path is reproduced, not known. Samanyu's 1e-11 finding is his measurement, so the 2e-11 floor is a guess with margin, and one real submission of a gate-green file is the only proof. The per-puzzle board source can change shape; the fetcher must fail loudly, not hand the scheduler an empty target map. The cron must not run heavy scoring on a box that a search is saturating: run it at nice 19 with a 4-process cap; scoring 1,000 n takes minutes.

tools.name: sqfleet: fleet job runner that spends CPU by expected gain per CPU-hour
tools.purpose: Replace the n%3 split and the gap-weighted random pick with one queue across boxB, boxA, boxF and boxD. The queue decides, per job, which puzzle, which method (FTMC, compose2, island transplant, polish) and which target side, based on what has actually paid per CPU-hour in similar puzzles. Dead cells stop getting CPU after a few hours; live ones get more.
tools.design: Python 3.12, stdlib plus numpy. A coordinator on boxA (sqlite: arms, jobs, leases, results) with an HTTP JSON API on the private network. Workers: one process per box (`sqfleet worker --slots K --max-load L`), pulling leases, running the engine as a subprocess at nice 19 in a scratch dir under <data> (box-local scratch on boxD), with a hard wall-clock kill, measuring CPU via resource.getrusage(RUSAGE_CHILDREN) (works on macOS and WSL, unlike Evan's /proc-based cpubudget), heartbeats every 30 s, and sinking any output into sqstore. Arms: (n, method, side_rung). The side ladder for n has rungs between our side and the target: L_k = ours - k/4 (ours - target) for k = 1..4, so partial gains count and the hardest rung is not the only goal. Job spec JSON: {n, method, L_target, seed, cpu_budget_s, parents:[packing ids], params}. Allocation: index = E[gain | success] x P(success per CPU-h), sampled by Thompson sampling. P has a hierarchical Gamma-Poisson prior pooled over cells (method x squares-short class {1,2,3} x regime (n hundred, frac band m+0.55..0.85 or not) x family id), so a sparse reward at one n informs its neighbours. Shaped reward, so the posterior moves before the first win: FTMC and compose2 report the best count |T| + fill reached at L_target; deficit reduction (n - count) earns graded credit (e.g. 0.3 for reaching n-1 at a rung that was n-2), and a certified win earns its actual score delta. Decay half-life of 48 h, because rates drift as the store fills. A 15% uniform floor keeps exploring. Event rules: when a win lands at n with fractional part f, queue transplant jobs at once for every n' whose target side has the same f within 1e-6 (the 791 -> 848/908/969 family) and for n+-1 drop/grow. A cap of 6 CPU-h per (n, method) per day stops one arm from eating the fleet. Ops: `sqfleet status`, `sqfleet pause <box>`, `sqfleet drain`, and a STOP file per box, matching the lane's habit. Engines are adapters: ftmc.py and compose2.py from Evan's clone (run from the clone, never copied, as with end_grind), stretch.py with the exact fill, and sqpack polish.
tools.expected_gain: +0.005 to +0.02 on top of what the engines find by 2027-01-17
tools.gain_reasoning: The engines, not the scheduler, close the gap: research puts FTMC+compose2 at 0.04-0.08 and transplant at 0.01-0.03. Against drive.py's gap-weighted random pick, the gain comes from three places. (1) Success varies by orders of magnitude across n and method; Evan's public toolchain trailed Kaggle's private bests even at n <= 324. A learned allocation typically finds 1.3-2x more wins per CPU-hour while the budget is short of what all 416 puzzles need, i.e. the first 2-4 weeks. (2) Family propagation turns one island win into 2-4 sibling wins within the hour, not whenever someone notices; the README caps family-wide gains at about 0.027 where we already hold a member. (3) The side ladder banks partial gains a fixed-target run throws away. Against 58k fleet CPU-hours to January, compute stops binding once a working method is known, so the edge shrinks over time. Hence 0.005-0.02, not more. If FTMC fails its positive control, this tool's gain is about 0.
tools.first_test: Two steps. (a) A simulator, 1 hour, on the laptop (no heavy work): 416 synthetic arms with the real gap distribution, where a hidden 10% of (n, method) pairs succeed at rate 0.2/CPU-h and the rest at 0.002. sqfleet must put more than 60% of spend on the live arms within 200 simulated CPU-hours, and a uniform gap-weighted picker must not. Negative control: with all arms equal, its spend must stay within 20% of uniform. (b) Real: once the lane hands over two boxes, a 48 h A/B on matched puzzle sets (stratified by hundred and squares-short class), same engines, bandit vs gap-weighted. Report wins, score delta and graded deficit reduction per CPU-h for each, with the raw counts. Expect few wins, so read the deficit metric first and say plainly if it is too noisy to call.
tools.risks: Rewards are sparse. Without the shaped deficit signal the posterior is just the prior, and the bandit equals random. FTMC and compose2 must expose their best count, which may need a small wrapper that parses their logs. Box contention: boxB pauses under load and other lanes share the boxes; leases must expire cleanly and a killed job must never write. The lane owns the boxes, so deployment waits for its handover; this design starts, stops and modifies nothing today. Evan's tools assume his pk store and his pool (no private pools rule); run them with tasks limit 1 per slot, or call their functions directly, so his pool and ours do not fight for cores. Overfitting cells too finely splits the data; start with about 40 cells and refine only when a cell has 20+ CPU-h.

tools.name: sqmap: gap atlas and spend dashboard
tools.purpose: Show where the gap is and where the CPU went, so the next engine we build targets the right regime. It also gives sqfleet its priors (squares-short class, family id) from one computation.
tools.design: Python plus a static HTML page (inline SVG, dark theme, no framework) written to logs/map/index.html on boxA and pulled to view, or rendered as a markdown table for the README Status. Data: sqstore best plus sqgate's refreshed targets plus sqfleet's job table. Views: (1) the triangle k = ceil(sqrt n), c = k^2 - n, one cell per n, coloured by gap in score units, with an overlay for the team holding the best; (2) squares-short per n: the largest n' < n whose certified side fits under the target side, which reproduces the 305/115/2 table and feeds sqfleet's prior; (3) fractional families: group target sides by frac to 1e-7 and list members we hold vs the leader's, with the smallest member first, e.g. the m+0.794 family starting at 299, ours 17.8010 vs 17.7936; (4) spend: CPU-h, wins, deficit reduction and score per CPU-h by method x regime cell, with the posterior mean and interval, so a dead method shows as dead; (5) a daily diff of the field from sqgate's board refresh. CLI: `sqmap build`, `sqmap families --top 30`, `sqmap short n`.
tools.expected_gain: 0 directly; decision value only
tools.gain_reasoning: It moves no square. Its use is choosing what to build next: if the spend view shows FTMC paying in the 1-short band regime and nothing in J-type jumbles above n=700, the next build day goes to a jumble-specific constructor instead of more FTMC CPU. With 416 puzzles and a flat gap (top 30 = 18.2%), guessing wrong about the regime wastes days, and this is the cheapest check against that. It also replaces the one-off scripts the research used, which nobody has rerun since 11-07.
tools.first_test: It must reproduce the checked numbers from our files: total per-puzzle gap 0.1704 over 416 puzzles, the top-12 list starting 971 (0.00135), 498 (0.00131), 593 (0.00128), Cats and boxes holding 0.146, and the squares-short table 305/115/2 from the research. Then a negative control: drop n=498 from the store, and its cell must show as missing (grid penalty), not as zero gap.
tools.risks: Low. The main risk is that it becomes the thing someone polishes instead of running searches; keep it to one page with no server. Family grouping at a 1e-7 frac tolerance can merge unrelated sides by coincidence; show the member count and treat singletons as noise. Never publish it outside the private repo or the private network, because it names other teams' per-puzzle positions only as far as the public board does, and it should stay ours.

critique.angle: Adversarial review of the four search-infrastructure tools (sqstore, sqgate, sqfleet, sqmap), checked against the lane's code and Evan's pk toolkit on boxA. I only read files there and touched nothing. Main finding: three of the four tools rebuild modules Evan's MIT repo already has on the box. That repo has ext/evand/search/packer/pk/store.py (a store with D4 canonical-hash dedup, sighting provenance and a frontier view), kaggle_import.py (Kaggle CSV into the store), pk/sink.py (adapters that import run outputs), pk/react.py (follow-up work queued on every new store row, which covers the family-propagation event rule), pk/events.py plus pk/bandit.py (scored claims and Thompson sampling per CPU-second), pk/tasks.py (the compute pool), pk/families.py plus familymap.py (the same k=ceil(sqrt n), c=k^2-n triangle and G/D/S/V/2/J family codes), pk/lab.py (wins, gain per CPU-h and paired comparison per arm), and pk/manifest.py (CPU measured with getrusage, so it works on macOS; only cpubudget.py reads /proc). The proposal's own numbers also undercut the scheduler: 58k fleet CPU-hours against 1k-8k per full FTMC pass means CPU is not the binding limit. The 'stale drop/grow seeds' bug is real (drive.py:143-144 reads current(state, n+-1) from the box's own state while --mod splits n by n%3), but drive.py is stopped (state-boxA/STOP dated 11-09 01:41, log line 'STOP file found, exiting' at 00:42Z), and the mode measured at about 1e-6 per CPU-hour is being retired, so fixing it buys nothing. One finding goes against the brief: neither floatsafe.py in the repo nor the copy on boxA enforces a 2e-11 minimum clearance. It tries centre dilations e = 0, then 1e-15 up to 1e-8, and stops at the first that the metric accepts, as written and after a pandas parse. A grep for '2e-11' or 'clear' finds nothing in either copy. So the hardening the research asked for (section 4) has not been done, and that is the one piece of sqgate worth building now. Overall: keep a slimmed sqgate (half a day). Drop sqstore, sqfleet and sqmap, and instead bring Evan's pk into use: import our 1,000 packings with kaggle_import.py and pk.py import, run his pool per box, and add a thin rsync of results from the other boxes into sink. Corrected total gain from this angle: about 0 to 0.005 plus insurance, not 0.005 to 0.02. Engine quality (FTMC's positive control) decides everything; none of these tools changes that.

verdicts.name: sqstore: central packing store with Kaggle-grade certification
verdicts.corrected_gain: about 0 (the 0.001-0.004 direct gain rests on drop/grow polish, which yields about 1e-6 per CPU-h and is being retired)
verdicts.reasons: 1) It duplicates pk/store.py on boxA. That store already keeps a packing table deduped by a D4 plus relabelling canonical hash, a sighting table for provenance with many sightings per packing, a status ladder (raw < screened < polished < certified / infeasible), parent lineage (pk/lineage.py), a frontier view, cached family codes (pk/families.py), and importers for Kaggle CSV (kaggle_import.py), many file formats (pk/packing.py parse) and run outputs (pk/sink.py). Saying it is 'written fresh so it does not depend on his schema' only adds a second store plus an export-pk bridge to keep in sync, which is more machinery, not less. 2) The direct gain is the stale-seed fix, and the seeds it fixes belong to drive.py's drop/grow modes (drive.py:140-146). drive.py has stopped and the research retires it, so the fix improves a dead engine. FTMC and compose2 read parents from Evan's store, not from state-*/best. 3) The one useful new field is the Kaggle-safety status (clear2e11_ok). That is a function, not a database: it belongs in floatsafe.py and the gate. 4) Building a stdlib HTTP POST /sink service on the private network, with spool and resend, is 1.5 days of plumbing for four boxes. rsync of result dirs into one box plus `pk.py import` does the same job.
verdicts.improvements: Do not build it. Instead, in about half a day: (a) import our 1,000 assembled packings and the harvest winners into Evan's store with kaggle_import.py, using a separate PK_STORE path so his tree stays untouched; (b) add one column or tag for Kaggle-safe status, filled by the gate's clearance check; (c) let the other boxes rsync their run dirs to boxA, where pk/sink.py imports them. Keep the D4 dedup negative control (a rotated and shuffled copy must give one id) as a test that his hash behaves as claimed on our data. Check that his store schema and tools run with an empty store before relying on them (the clone's runs/ holds only known110*.json, so his 1.7 M-row store is not there).

verdicts.name: sqgate: auto re-assembly, float-safe certification, scoring and leaderboard diff
verdicts.corrected_gain: 0 in packings; it prevents a Kaggle rejection like Samanyu's 1e-12 case (about 0.1 on his file) and any per-n regression on upload
verdicts.reasons: The 2e-11 floor is not in place. floatsafe.py (both the repo copy and the boxA copy) uses EPS = [0] + 1e-15..1e-8 and stops at the first dilation that the local metric accepts after a pandas parse. That is exactly the case Samanyu says Kaggle rejected (1e-12 gaps, 22.26 locally against 22.36 on Kaggle). drive.py dilates by only 1e-12. So the risk the research flagged in section 4 is still open, and this tool's core check is new value, not duplication. But it is inflated: the 25.97 failure is already fixed by floatsafe.py plus pdscore.py plus the README rule, and re-assembly with assemble.py already exists. A launchd cron every 15 minutes is unneeded while nothing is producing gains and submissions are manual (at most 10 a day). Evan has satcheck_f64.py (an independent SAT check) and dilate_cert.py, which can serve as a second independent checker. The 'replay history' test is good: assembled-2026-11-08.csv and floatsafe-2026-11-08.csv are both on boxA in gather/.
verdicts.improvements: Cut it to a half-day script, gate.py. (1) Add a min-clearance pass to floatsafe.py: an exact SAT gap per pair in float64 after the pandas read, on candidate pairs from a grid hash. Dilate centres until min gap >= 2e-11 instead of stopping at the first metric pass. Cross-check with Evan's satcheck_f64 logic. (2) Diff per n against the last submitted file: refuse any per-n regression and any rise in total. (3) Write candidate.json with sha256, total and the n that moved. (4) Refresh the board on demand with harvest_fetch, never on a cron, and fail loudly on an empty or changed schema. Drop the 15-minute launchd job. Tests: the 11-08 assembled file must go RED; the floatsafe file must stay GREEN at 22.2223365223 or within 1e-6 of it after the 2e-11 floor; a +1e-12 nudge must go RED on clearance; a 0.01 regression at n=10 must go RED. The only real proof is one Kaggle submission of a gate-green file, so plan for it (Sergio's call).

verdicts.name: sqfleet: fleet job runner that spends CPU by expected gain per CPU-hour
verdicts.corrected_gain: 0 to 0.005, and 0 if FTMC fails its positive control (the proposal admits this)
verdicts.reasons: 1) By the proposal's own numbers, CPU does not bind (58k fleet CPU-h against 1k-8k per full pass over 416 puzzles). Smart allocation only pays when the budget is short of the demand, so the edge is a few weeks of front-loading at most. 2) '1.3-2x more wins per CPU-hour' has no source, and wins are sparse. The proposal's own risk section concedes that without the shaped deficit signal the bandit equals random. Neither FTMC nor compose2 reports a 'best count |T|+fill at L_target' through any interface we have checked; that needs a log-parsing wrapper that has not been scoped. A hierarchical Gamma-Poisson prior over about 40 cells needs dozens of wins to move, and the lane does not have them yet. 3) It duplicates Evan's machinery: pk/bandit.py (Thompson sampling per CPU-second with decay and a floor, the same design), pk/events.py (claims scored per (parent, move)), pk/react.py (rules that queue follow-up units on new store rows, so 'on a win at frac f, queue transplants' is one @rule), pk/tasks.py (pool with priorities and `repeat --budget`), and pk/manifest.py (getrusage CPU, which works on macOS). The /proc limitation applies only to cpubudget.py. 4) Three days for a coordinator, leases, heartbeats, an HTTP API and adapters across four boxes, one of them WSL behind wsl.exe, is optimistic. The boxF launch trap in the README alone shows how fragile cross-box process control is. 5) The side-ladder idea (bank partial gains) is the one new idea, and it is a parameter of the FTMC job, not a reason for a scheduler.
verdicts.improvements: Do not build it until FTMC passes the remove-one-square positive control and gives a measured win rate per CPU-h. Then use the smallest form: run Evan's pk/tasks.py on each box, each with a static work list. Order the list family-first (smallest member of each frac family first, e.g. 299 for m+0.794 and 791 for m+0.606) and within that by gap. Add one pk/react.py rule that queues transplant jobs for same-frac siblings and n+-1 when a win lands. Pass the side ladder (rungs between our side and the target) as an FTMC goal argument. Collect results with rsync. That is about half a day. If after two weeks the per-method win rates differ by an order of magnitude across regimes, then consider weighting, using his bandit.py, not a new one.

verdicts.name: sqmap: gap atlas and spend dashboard
verdicts.corrected_gain: 0 (decision value only, and most of it is already available)
verdicts.reasons: 1) Its triangle view (k = ceil(sqrt n), c = k^2 - n) and family codes are exactly what Evan's familymap.py and pk/families.py do (G/D/S/V/2/J codes, cached per packing). The spend view per method and regime with wins and gain per CPU-h is pk/lab.py's `pk.py try --report` (per arm x n: tries, wins, best gain, gain/CPU-h, paired comparison against a control). 2) The squares-short table and the gap by hundreds have just been computed for the research doc (305/115/2, 0.1704, the top-12 list) and sit in results/ TSVs. Recomputing them as an HTML page is polish on analysis that already exists. 3) There is no spend data to show until a search runs, so view (4) is empty at first. 4) The proposal itself names the risk that it becomes the thing someone polishes instead of running searches.
verdicts.improvements: Skip the dashboard. If anything, add a two-hour script, shortmap.py, that writes one TSV per refresh: n, our side, target side, squares-short, frac family to 1e-7 with member count, and the holding team. That feeds the family-first work list above and the README Status. Its only new parts compared with familymap are the squares-short count against the Kaggle target and frac grouping on the leader's sides. Its first test (reproduce 0.1704, 305/115/2, and n=971 first at 0.00135) is the right one.

design.angle: Wild and unconventional tools: read the leader's structure from the public 10-digit sides, put the four idle Apple M4 GPUs to work, evolve band constructors without an LLM, and add a small learned prior over moves. Grounding I checked: our gap to the per-puzzle board is 0.1704, and 0.163 of it is on n where our side and the best side have the same integer part, so the whole fight is in the fractional part (the seam or island). The per-puzzle board gives sides to about 1e-10 (791 Cats 28.60588450854, 908 KuanHaoChen 30.60588450857). boxB, boxA and boxD are all Apple M4, 10 cores, 16 GB. Their GPUs sit idle while the lane uses the CPUs. Evan's repo on boxA already has an LLM prompt-evolution of constructors (evolve2: blind ties at n=234/235, nothing past 236), band moves (movegen.py), Mondrian composition and a family map. The tools below are built to do what those do not.

tools.name: sidefinger: identify the leader's island structure from its published side
tools.purpose: The per-puzzle board publishes every best side to about 10 reliable digits. A rigid band packing's side is fixed exactly by its contact graph, so a 10-digit fractional part works as a fingerprint of that structure. sidefinger enumerates candidate seam structures, solves each one exactly, and looks for a structure whose side matches the leader's fractional part to 1e-9. A match tells us which structure to build at that side, and the same structure carries to every member of its family (791/848/908/969, 498/803, 842/901/962 ...). We never need their coordinates.
tools.design: Language: Python 3.12 with mpmath (40-digit Newton solves and PSLQ) and numpy, plus a small Rust crate (PyO3) for the float64 pre-screen. Three stages. (1) Target table: from per-puzzle-lb JSON (refresh it first), per n: L*, m=floor(L*), f=L*-m, n-m^2, and the family key round(f,9). Group n by key: 254 families today, and the top 30 carry 34% of the gap. (2) Structure grammar, an IslandSpec dataclass: corner pair (BR/TL or BL/TR), two integer staircase step vectors a[], b[] (the upright row lengths each grid gives up along the diagonal), a rung list of (single|pair, contact pattern: which staircase corner each rung touches), and optional junction slips. Each spec gives a square system of contact equations in unknowns (theta_i, rung offsets, f). The equations are point-on-edge SAT contacts between unit squares and with the integer staircase corners, so the upright grid enters only as integer constants. (3) Solver: float64 Newton from 64 angle seeds (Rust, about 20 us per solve), keep the converged roots with f in (0,1), then refine the survivors to 40 digits in mpmath and check the Jacobian rank (rigidity). Index: a sorted array of f, so matching is a binary search at tolerance 2e-10. Side channel: mpmath.pslq on [f, 1, sqrt2, sqrt3, sqrt5, sqrt7] and on cos/sin of candidate angles, with max coefficient 40. That catches closed forms like 15+(sqrt7-1)/2 (Evan's 234 family) and 19+4/7 (364). On a hit: build the full packing at side m+f for every family member with gen.mis_fill2 / fillfast for the uprights, then fq polish, then score.py and floatsafe.py (2e-11 clearance). Interface: `sidefinger enumerate --rungs 8..40 --steps-max 6 --out idx.npz`, `sidefinger match --targets lb.json --idx idx.npz > hits.tsv` (n, f, spec_json, residual), `sidefinger build --hit hits.tsv:row --n 791,848,908,969 --out cand/`. The output goes to cand/<n>.txt in Evan's text format, which the lane imports through its existing harvest_apply path.
tools.expected_gain: 0.005 to 0.025, most likely about 0.01
tools.gain_reasoning: A match is decisive, because it hands us the structure to build at the exact best side, for every member of a family at once. The families give it leverage: the top 30 hold about 0.058 of the gap and the 0.6059 family alone holds 0.0031 over 3 n. What limits it is coverage. Our grammar has to contain the leader's seam. The evidence from n=498 and n=593 (several rung angles, relaxed against each other) and from Evan's 236-240 (interlocking staircase blocks) says many large-n islands are not short single-band specs. I assume we hit 20-40% of the top-30 families and 5-10% of the 146 singleton families (0.060). That gives 0.012-0.023 + 0.003-0.006 before overlap with FTMC, and I discount for overlap. False matches are controlled: 1e7 structures at 2e-10 tolerance give about 0.004 expected chance hits per target, and every hit must still certify n squares.
tools.first_test: Positive control on structures we already hold at the best side: n=364 (19+4/7, ours matches to 2.5e-11) and a 234-family member (15+(sqrt7-1)/2). Hide our coordinates, run enumerate+match, and require that sidefinger recovers f to 1e-9 and builds a packing that certifies at that side. Negative control: feed 1,000 random f in (0.5,0.9) and require zero certified builds. Then the live test: the 0.6059 family (791/848/908; we hold .6370295589, the same family with a worse island). A hit at 791 would show at once at 908 as well.
tools.risks: The grammar may miss the real seams (several angles, junction slips). Then it finds nothing, cheaply, and I would know within the first 2 days from the control and the 0.6059 test. The side may depend on contacts far from the seam (staircase bending), so the local equations come out slightly wrong. The fix is to fall back to the 1e-6 match as a seed for FTMC rather than demanding a 1e-9 match. Leader sides carry their own dilation of about 1e-11 to 1e-10, so matching tighter than 2e-10 is meaningless. The per-puzzle board is a public third-party notebook, and using published sides is legitimate, but we should cite it.

tools.name: metalquench: batched FTMC quench on the idle Apple M4 GPUs (MLX custom Metal kernels)
tools.purpose: Evan's own log says the FTMC/evolve evaluator bottleneck is the quench (13-26 min per eval under load), not the fill (58 ms with fillfast). The lane's CPUs are full, and the four M4 GPUs (10-core, about 4 TFLOPS fp32 each) do nothing. metalquench runs thousands of fixed-side penalty relaxations at once on the GPU, so FTMC's count search ('fit n squares at side L*') gets several times more proposals per day on hardware we are not using.
tools.design: Language: Python on Apple MLX, with mx.fast.metal_kernel for the hot loop and plain MLX ops elsewhere. No Swift app. Data layout: a structure-of-arrays batch [R replicas, N squares] of (x, y, theta) in fp32, plus a per-replica side L and a uniform-grid cell list rebuilt every 16 steps (cell size 1.42, at most 12 squares per cell, R*N*12 int16). Kernel 1, pair penalty: for each square and each neighbour in its 3x3 cells, a 4-axis SAT penetration depth p, energy sum max(p,0)^2 and its analytic gradient in x, y and theta, with wall penalties on the 4 sides. One thread per (replica, square); 32-replica threadgroups share nothing, so there is no atomic contention. Kernel 2: FIRE minimiser steps (velocity Verlet with adaptive dt), about 2,000 steps per quench. The host loop is a replica-exchange Metropolis over FTMC moves on the tilted set only (perturb, add or remove a rung, transfer a rung between bands, rotate a band by a few degrees), in batches of R=512 proposals. Survivors (energy < 1e-8 in fp32) go to the CPU, where the existing Rust fq does the f64 polish, then score.py and floatsafe.py. The GPU never certifies anything. Interface: `metalquench run --start pk.txt --n 498 --side 22.80 --replicas 512 --hours 4 --out cand/`, plus a Python API `quench(batch: mx.array, L: mx.array) -> (batch, energy)`, so FTMC/compose2 can call it in place of their packer subprocess.
tools.expected_gain: 0.0 directly. It multiplies the lane's FTMC idea (0.04-0.08). My estimate of the extra beyond CPU-only FTMC is 0.005-0.02.
tools.gain_reasoning: Throughput: one replica at n=800 costs about 800*12*60 flops per gradient, about 0.6 MFLOP, so at 10% of 4 TFLOPS that is about 700k gradient steps/s per box, roughly 350 quenches/s at 2,000 steps. One CPU core of fq does about one quench every few seconds. That makes one M4 GPU worth about 20-60 CPU cores of quench, and 4 boxes add the equivalent of 80-240 cores on top of the lane's 24 threads. But there is a precedent against raw compute: Samanyu's CUDA annealing 'hit the same plateau'. More quenches only help when the move set can change the count, which is FTMC's tilted-set moves plus exact refill, and not plain annealing. So the gain is FTMC's gain multiplied by a log of throughput. If FTMC finds wins at a rate that scales like log(proposals), 5-10x more proposals adds roughly 15-30% to FTMC's yield, that is +0.005-0.02.
tools.first_test: Correctness: on 200 random and 50 record configurations, the GPU energy and gradient must match a float64 numpy reference to 1e-5 relative. Mutate one sign in the SAT kernel and check that the test goes red. Power test, the one the band-end grinder failed: remove one square from our n=803 (and a tilted one from n=498), run at the original side for 30 GPU-minutes, and require the count back with an fq-certified packing. Benchmark: quenches per second at n=500 and n=900 against fq on one core of the same box, reported as measured. Only after that, 4 GPU-hours on n=498 at side 22.81.
tools.risks: fp32 accumulates error in boxes of side 30, so contacts look feasible at 1e-6 and fail f64 polish. Mitigation: positions relative to cell origins, and every survivor polished in f64. MLX custom kernels are young and may need a Metal-cpp fallback (+2 days). GPU work still uses memory bandwidth and some CPU on a box the lane owns, so it needs the lane's OK before any run. Most important: if FTMC itself does not beat the CPU-only rate on 498/593, this tool multiplies zero, so build it only after FTMC's first test reports a positive gain per CPU-hour.

tools.name: seamgp: LLM-free grammatical evolution of band constructors, selected across a whole family
tools.purpose: Evan's LLM prompt-evolution (evolve2) tied two hidden records blind (234, 235) but never built the interlocking staircase blocks that 236-240 and the large-n leaders use, and the LLM count proxies were off by 10-15. seamgp evolves small typed constructor programs whose genome encodes the staircases directly, and it scores each program on every member of a fractional family at once (n = m^2 + k as m grows). Selection then favours a seam that scales with m, which is exactly what the leader's shared fractional parts show.
tools.design: Language: Rust for the decoder and the fast evaluator, with a Python driver (PyO3). Genome: a typed tree in a small DSL. Leaves are Staircase(corner, steps: Vec<u8>), Band(angle_deg, rungs: u8, pair_mask: u32, inset), Slip(pos, angle) and Block(w, h, angle). Combinators are Seam(Staircase, Band, Staircase), Stack(Band, Band, junction_offset), Mirror(axis) and Transpose. Decoding is deterministic: lay out the uprights on the four corner lattices at side L = m + f_target, place the tilted parts, drop overlaps greedily, then refill uprights with fillfast/mis_fill2 (called through Evan's gen.py, or ported to Rust). Fitness for a family F = {(n_j, m_j)} at target fraction f: for each member, count = squares certified after a 200-step quench (metalquench if it exists, fq otherwise). The score is the mean shortfall of n_j - count_j, ties broken by the side reached after a short shrink. Search: MAP-Elites, with an archive keyed by (tilted count bucket, band count 1-3, mean angle bin of 5 degrees) for diversity, and mutation operators that edit step vectors (+-1 on a step, insert or delete a step), flip pair_mask bits, nudge angles by +-2 degrees, and swap subtrees between elites. 64 islands, migration every 50 generations. Interface: `seamgp evolve --family 0.6059 --targets lb.json --gens 2000 --out runs/fam6059/`, which writes archive.jsonl (genome, per-member counts) and cand/<n>.txt for any member at full count at a side below ours.
tools.expected_gain: 0.005 to 0.02, most likely about 0.008
tools.gain_reasoning: The method only applies where a family has two or more members. The top-30 families hold about 0.058 of the gap, and multi-member families as a whole hold more than the singletons' 0.060. A genome that fits one member transfers to the others, so one win is worth 2-4 n (0.6059: 0.0031 over 791/848/908). Evan's blind reproduction rate gives the prior: 2 of 7 hidden n tied, and none of the hard interlocking ones. Our genome makes interlocking expressible, but whether that is enough is unproven. I assume 10-25% of the top 30 families reach the best side, about 0.006-0.015, plus a little from singletons where the evolved program alone is the seed for FTMC. It overlaps with sidefinger: both target the same families, and sidefinger's hits can seed the population.
tools.first_test: Holdout reproduction, like Evan's gen-1 protocol but on our own data: take a family where we already hold the best side at two or more n, hide those packings, evolve for 2 CPU-hours, and require the hidden side reproduced within 1e-7. Report the reproduction rate over 5 such families. As a negative control, a genome with random step vectors must never reach full count at those sides; if it does, the evaluator is lying. Then the real target: 0.6059 (791/848/908) and 0.7939 (498/803) at the leader's sides, 8 CPU-hours each.
tools.risks: The structures may be more irregular than the DSL (several angles relaxed against each other at 498/593), and then evolution plateaus 3-6 squares short, as our rigid bandseed did at 492/498. Fitness is noisy under load (Evan saw +-0.02 normalised), which stalls selection. Mitigation: a fixed quench budget, deterministic seeds, and re-evaluating elites. CPU is the scarce resource on the fleet, so seamgp competes with FTMC for the lane's threads unless metalquench carries its quench.

tools.name: moveprior: a contextual bandit over structural moves, trained on record lineages
tools.purpose: FTMC and movegen choose moves (add or remove a rung, transfer, row_add, shift, rotate, drop_J) uniformly or by hand-set weights. We have a free training set of improving moves nobody has mined: the record lineage across the jlevy register history, Couzo's git history, the 5,747 harvested files (many versions per n), Evan's chain_lineage.py and the lane's improvements.tsv. moveprior learns which move type, at which place, improved which kind of packing, and biases the proposals.
tools.design: Language: Python, with numpy and scikit-learn (gradient-boosted trees, no deep model; the data is a few thousand transitions at most). Data harvester: for every pair (older, newer) of packings at the same n with newer side < older, compute the Hungarian matching over the 8 container symmetries (as rediscover.py does), then classify the edit into the movegen vocabulary with its locus (junction, band end, staircase step, interior). Features: n, m, k=n-m^2, f, tilted count, band count and angles (from familymap's classification), the locus's local density, and the gap to the board. Model: P(improve | move type, locus, features). At run time, Thompson sampling with that model as the prior and online updates from the lane's own accept and reject logs. Interface: a Python function `propose(packing_features) -> list[(move, locus, weight)]`, which movegen/FTMC read through a single --prior weights.json, and `moveprior fit --lineage dirs... --out model.pkl`.
tools.expected_gain: 0.0 directly. It is an efficiency multiplier of about 1.2-2x on FTMC and movegen. In score terms, at most 0.002-0.008.
tools.gain_reasoning: Honest framing: improving transitions above n=300 are scarce. Most of the public lineage is below 324, and the private frontier is invisible to us, so the model learns the small-n regime and transfers weakly. A good prior saves proposals; it does not create new basins. Its value is the FTMC yield times the efficiency gain times a log factor, the same argument as metalquench but smaller.
tools.first_test: Offline time split: train on transitions dated before 2026-10-20 and test on the later ones. The prior must rank the actual improving move type in its top 3 more often than uniform (6 types, so 50%) by at least 15 points, with a bootstrap interval. Shuffled-label control: the same pipeline on permuted labels must fall to about 50%. If it fails the split, drop it.
tools.risks: Too few above-300 transitions to learn anything, and the time-split test catches that within day 1. Classifying the edit from a matched pair is error-prone when the whole packing reorganises, as Evan saw with one-extra-square reorganisations. Lowest priority of the four; build it only if FTMC runs at scale.

critique.angle: Adversarial review of the "wild tools" proposal: sidefinger, metalquench, seamgp and moveprior. I checked each claim against the lane's files and Evan's clone on boxA (read-only). One fact sinks most of the proposal. I recomputed the families from results/per-puzzle-lb-2026-11-09.json against results/assembled-2026-11-08-per-n.tsv. Total gap 0.1715. When the fractional part has to match to 1e-6, so that two puzzles really share one structure, families with two or more members hold only 0.012 of it (0.011 at 1e-9, 0.031 at 1e-4). The 254-family figure, with the top 30 holding 34%, only appears at about 1e-3 rounding (0.112 multi-member). At that tolerance the members are different packings. The "0.794 family" sides are 299 .79364, 454 .79358, 498 .79386, 544 .79413, 747 .79376, 803 .79394, so they differ in the 4th digit and no single seam spec gives them all. Only 791 and 908 match to 3e-11 (gap 0.0021). 848 (.6058838) and 969 (.6055709) are different structures, and 842/901/962 (0.0019) is the next exact family. So the "one win carries to 2-4 n" leverage behind sidefinger and seamgp mostly does not exist. Other checks: there are 3 M4 boxes (boxB, boxA, boxD; boxF is Intel), not 4. Evan's FTMC has never run here: search/packer/target/release is empty on boxA, so every multiplier tool is multiplying an unmeasured base. FTMC already has the structural moves (delete tilted, add a lattice neighbour, shift a channel group, re-angle) and an exact fill (fillfast, about 58 ms). Evan's "13-26 min per eval" was his LLM evolve2 evaluator on a loaded machine, not an FTMC step.

verdicts.name: sidefinger: identify the leader's island structure from its published side
verdicts.corrected_gain: 0 to 0.003 (most likely about 0). The leverage case falls apart: exact multi-member families hold 0.011-0.012 of the gap, not 0.058 for the top 30.
verdicts.reasons: (1) Family leverage is mostly an artefact of 1e-3 clustering. At 1e-9, where a fingerprint means anything, only 0.0107 of the 0.1715 gap sits in multi-member families. 848 and 969 are not in the 791/908 family (they differ at 7e-7 and 3e-4). (2) The leader's sides inside a 1e-3 'family' differ in the 4th digit. That shows the side depends on how the whole staircase and the uprights relax, not on a local seam whose uprights enter as integer constants. The grammar's core assumption (uprights exactly on corner lattices, side fixed by local contacts) is therefore false for the large-n records that make up the gap. (3) A 10-digit match to a 1e7-spec grammar is not decisive. With about 1e7 continuous-parameter specs and Newton roots, chance collisions at 2e-10 are possible, and the proposal's own risk section already falls back to '1e-6 seed for FTMC'. That means FTMC at L*, which idea 1 already does with the board's side. (4) Even a correct structure still has to be built and certified at m+f with n squares, which is the hard part, and FTMC and compose2 do that step. (5) 5 days for the grammar, a Rust PyO3 Newton pre-screen, mpmath refinement, PSLQ and the builder is optimistic. 10+ days is more realistic, and it is unlikely to pass its own 0.6059 live test. The positive control on 364 (19+4/7) and the 234 family is a small-n closed form and says nothing about n >= 300.
verdicts.improvements: Cut it to a half-day analyser and skip the engine. Recompute families at 1e-9 on a refreshed board, list the exact multi-member families (791/908, 842/901/962, 530/577, 902/963 ...) and run PSLQ on those sides only. Use the result for scheduling: build the smaller member with FTMC and transplant to the others (idea 2). Do not build the structure enumerator unless PSLQ finds closed forms at n >= 300.

verdicts.name: metalquench: batched FTMC quench on the idle Apple M4 GPUs (MLX custom Metal kernels)
verdicts.corrected_gain: 0 now. 0 to 0.005 if FTMC first shows a positive yield per CPU-hour and the relax/squeeze share of an FTMC step is measured as dominant.
verdicts.reasons: (1) It multiplies an unmeasured base. FTMC has not been built or run here (search/packer/target/release is empty on boxA), so the 'FTMC 0.04-0.08' it multiplies is a guess, and the proposal already gates itself on that. (2) The bottleneck it cites is wrong. '13-26 min per eval' is Evan's evolve2 LLM-constructor evaluator under load (evolve2/LOG.md line 36/49), not an FTMC step. Nobody has measured how an FTMC step splits across perturb, packer relax, fillfast and penalty squeeze. (3) Amdahl's law: FTMC's step runs relax T, then a fillfast exact fill (CPU, about 58 ms), then a squeeze, then Metropolis. Only the relax and squeeze move to the GPU, and the fill and the host Python loop stay on CPUs the lane already saturates, so 20-60 cores of 'quench' cannot turn into 20-60x FTMC proposals. (4) The 'one CPU quench every few seconds' and '350 quenches/s per GPU' figures are unmeasured, and the fp32 penalty energy floor of 1e-8 at side 30 is too coarse for the final contacts, so every survivor still needs a CPU f64 squeeze. (5) The hardware is 3 M4 GPUs, not 4. Using them runs on boxes the lane owns and needs its OK. (6) Samanyu's CUDA annealing hitting the same plateau is direct evidence that raw quench throughput does not add squares.
verdicts.improvements: Build nothing until FTMC runs. Then spend 1 hour profiling one FTMC step on n=498 (time in packer relax, fillfast, squeeze). Only if relax plus squeeze is over 70% of the step and FTMC has found at least one count win per N CPU-hours: prototype the pair-penalty kernel in MLX in 1 day, gated by the f64-reference gradient test and its sign-mutation red check, and move FTMC's batched relax onto it. Keep the API as a drop-in for run_packer('relax'), so FTMC needs no rewrite.

verdicts.name: seamgp: LLM-free grammatical evolution of band constructors, selected across a whole family
verdicts.corrected_gain: 0 to 0.004. The family-selection premise is gone: exact multi-member families hold about 0.012 of the gap.
verdicts.reasons: (1) Its fitness, mean shortfall over the members of a family at target fraction f, assumes the members share f. At the precision that decides the score they mostly do not (0.794 'family' members differ by up to 6e-4). So it either optimises a coarse f that is not each member's best side, or shrinks back to the per-n search FTMC, compose2 and Evan's evolve2 already do. (2) It duplicates Evan's toolchain: mondrian.py (composition), movegen.py (band add/del/transfer/row/shift/rotate/drop_J on band lattices), compose2 (two corner pieces plus exact fill) and evolve2. The novel parts are only the DSL and MAP-Elites. (3) The lane's own evidence argues against rigid typed constructors at n >= 300. The rigid bandseed stops at 492/498 and 589/593, and the README says the real channels hold squares at several angles relaxed against each other. The DSL's Band(angle, rungs) plus Staircase(steps) is again a rigid grammar, and evolve2 could not build the interlocking 236-240 blocks either. (4) 6 days for a Rust decoder, DSL, MAP-Elites, 64 islands and a fill port is optimistic, and it competes for the same saturated CPUs as FTMC. (5) The holdout control needs families where we hold the best side at 2+ n at n >= 300. Our exact-family data shows almost none exist, so the control would run at small n, which is irrelevant to the gap.
verdicts.improvements: If anything survives, fold the useful bit into idea 2 (island transplant with exact fill) for the handful of exact families (791/908, 842/901/962, 530/577, 902/963): evolve or search the smallest member once, then transplant with fillfast. That needs no DSL or GP engine and is half a day on top of stretch.py.

verdicts.name: moveprior: a contextual bandit over structural moves, trained on record lineages
verdicts.corrected_gain: about 0 (at most 0.002); the proposal itself rates it lowest
verdicts.reasons: (1) There is no base yet: FTMC and movegen have not run on our boxes, so there are no accept/reject logs to learn from online. (2) The training set is wrong for the gap. Public lineages are almost all below n=324, the frontier at n >= 300 is private, and our improvements.tsv holds only a handful of sqpack polish wins (502, 587, 803, 855, 923), which are side shrinks, not count-adding structural moves. (3) Classifying a before/after pair into movegen's vocabulary with Hungarian matching breaks down exactly where it matters, when one extra square reorganises the packing (evolve2 LOG). (4) FTMC's 7 move kinds are cheap, so uniform sampling over them wastes little, and a 1.2-2x efficiency gain on an unknown yield is noise. (5) The time-split test needs more transitions dated after 10-20 than we have at n >= 300.
verdicts.improvements: Drop it. If FTMC runs at scale, log per-move-kind accept rates and reweight by hand from those counts (a 10-line change to ftmc.perturb's rng.randrange(7)). That gets most of the value without a harvester or a model.
